sections.title: Start here: the storage specialist a bank built
ps: In 2021 Goldman Sachs Asset Management wanted to own standalone batteries and could not find a developer it wanted to back, so it bought a project in Goleta, hired a chief executive and built a company around it. GridStor is that company: a {{sponsor-created platform}} that owns 280 MW of contracted batteries, is building 250 MW more, and has bought five projects from other developers in eighteen months. This guide teaches how an {{asset manager}}'s {{infrastructure fund}} deploys money into storage, what a sponsor-backed specialist can finance that a founder-led one cannot, how a battery bought at notice-to-proceed is contracted before it is built, and where the model fails.

**What it deliberately does not repeat:** the Aypa guide teaches the contracted platform as an asset a buyer prices; the Spearmint guide teaches the merchant developer and financing a battery with no PPA; the Invenergy guide teaches the diversified developer and its owners; the Available Power guide teaches the seller side of the late-stage market GridStor buys in. The Classroom owns how a battery earns money hour by hour.

**One idea carries the guide.** A fund is a clock with money in it. It must invest, it must show returns, and one day it must get out. Every choice GridStor makes — buy late-stage projects instead of originating, contract every asset, borrow from one bank that already knows the sponsor, hire a trading desk to convert merchant revenue into fixed payments — is the choice a fund makes when it wants storage cash flow on a fund's schedule.

sections.title: How an asset manager's fund owns a developer
ps: An {{asset manager}} runs money for others. Goldman Sachs Asset Management raises funds from {{limited partner}}s — pensions, insurers, sovereign funds — and its {{general partner}} team decides where the money goes and earns a fee plus a share of the profits. When lenders say GridStor 'is owned by funds managed by Goldman Sachs Asset Management', the owners are the fund's investors and the decision-maker is the fund's investment committee, on which one GridStor board member sits.

**The vehicle.** The company never names it; trade press calls it Horizon Energy Storage, a fund managed by GSAM's Sustainability and Infrastructure investing groups. The media kit says GSAM 'has raised over $1 billion to invest in energy storage assets that GridStor will source and manage' — the fund owns the batteries, GridStor finds and runs them. The fund's own 2023 close of a different vehicle (Horizon Environment & Climate Solutions I) does not mention GridStor, which is why the sponsor's commitment to this company is genuinely unknown.

**Creation, not investment.** Latitude Media's account is that Goldman 'created' GridStor after failing to find a developer to back, having already bought the Goleta project; Chris Taylor was hired to assemble the team. That inverts the usual order — a founder builds a pipeline and then sells a stake — and it explains the company's shape: no founder equity to dilute, no legacy pipeline, a board with two GSAM investors and a retired Goldman partner, and a chief executive who spent seven years investing Google's clean-energy money rather than developing projects.

**What a fund wants from a developer.** Assets with cash flow a fund can hold and, eventually, sell: contracted, financed, operating batteries. Not options. That is the difference between GridStor's boilerplate — 'focused on contracted revenues' — and Spearmint's, and it is the reason the next section is about buying rather than originating.

sections.title: Why buy instead of originate
ps: Originating a project — finding land, filing an interconnection request, waiting through the studies, winning the permit — takes four to seven years and produces mostly options that expire. A fund with a {{fund life}} cannot spend its first five years waiting. Buying at or near {{ready-to-build}} converts the sponsor's money into an operating battery in eighteen to twenty-four months: Hidden Lakes was bought in March 2024 and operating in November 2025.

**What the buyer pays for.** The rungs the seller has climbed — {{site control}}, a {{queue position}} with studies done, a permit, sometimes a contract (White Tank came with its 20-year APS toll). The seller's return is the difference between what those rungs cost and what a buyer with cheaper capital will pay; Available Power's whole business was to be that seller.

**What the buyer must still do.** Contract it if it is not contracted, sign the EPC and supply agreements, finance it, build it. GridStor's team is built for exactly those steps — a CTO who ran EPC contracting and procurement at Clearway, an SVP of EPC from Goldman Sachs Renewable Power, a VP of Origination from Ørsted, a head of capital markets from Greenbacker — and not for the years of origination the sellers do.

**Why the pipeline number moves.** 'Over 5 GW' in September 2025 became 'over 3 GW' two months later. A pipeline of acquired and optioned projects is re-scoped as options lapse or are dropped; a buyer's pipeline is a shopping list, not a promise. The company also says it develops greenfield — Goleta and Santa Fe Springs are in-house — but every asset since 2023 was bought.

sections.title: What a sponsor can finance that a founder cannot
ps: A founder-led developer borrows on its projects; a sponsor-owned one borrows on its projects *and* on the sponsor's name. GridStor's disclosed financings show what that buys.

**One lender that keeps coming back.** NORD/LB lent USD 55 million on Goleta in 2023 — the bank's fourth standalone battery in the country — then long-term debt on the same project, a USD 50 million {{letter-of-credit facility}} for the development pipeline in 2025, and half of the USD 120 million Gunnar package in 2026. A repeat lender prices the second deal on the first; the sponsor's ownership is what let the first deal happen a year after founding.

**A development letter-of-credit facility.** Interconnection deposits and contract security are posted with letters of credit; a corporate facility for them (USD 50 million) is something a bank writes for a company whose owner is a fund, not for a three-year-old developer on its own. Aypa's equivalent tranche was USD 550 million — the scale difference between a Blackstone platform and a Goldman one.

**Credit transfers at the front of the queue.** Goleta's credits were sold to J.P. Morgan in one of the first battery transfers under the 2022 law, at what Latitude Media reports as 'ninety something cents' per dollar; Hidden Lakes' USD 86 million went to Foss & Company. A sponsor's counsel and relationships get a small company into a market that large buyers prefer to enter with large sellers.

**{{tax-equity bridge loan}}s and construction debt** at Gunnar from NORD/LB and Siemens Financial Services, and a First Citizens loan at Hidden Lakes, sized to be repaid when the credit buyer funds at commercial operation. Each is ordinary project finance; what is not ordinary is closing them serially with two lenders' first storage deals (Siemens Financial Services' first with GridStor; First Citizens as lead agent) on a company with no track record beyond one 60 MW battery.

**What the sponsor does not do.** It does not guarantee the debt — every facility is at the project — and it has not, on the record, committed a stated sum. 'Deployed only a fraction of the capital that we originally raised' (Taylor, June 2025) is the closest the record comes to saying how much is behind the company.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The clock and the contract disagree.** A fund's {{fund life}} is ten to twelve years; White Tank's toll is twenty and Goleta's RA contract seventeen. The assets will be sold before the contracts end — to another fund, a utility or a platform buyer — and the price then depends on a market the sponsor does not control. The exit route is nowhere in the record.

**Nothing the sponsor has committed is public.** 'Over $1 billion raised' for a strategy is not a commitment to this company, and 'deployed only a fraction' can mean patience or hesitation. A lender lending on the sponsor's name is lending on a name, not a number.

**One lender is a strength until it is not.** NORD/LB is in four of five disclosed transactions. A repeat lender is cheap and fast; a lender that changes its view of US storage — or of the sponsor — takes the pipeline's financing with it.

**A bought pipeline can be un-bought.** 'Over 5 GW' became 'over 3 GW' in two months; the Oklahoma and Capacity Power Group projects have had no update in eighteen months; the 2022 Los Angeles Basin portfolio has produced one named project and a court ruling against batteries in unincorporated Los Angeles County hangs over the rest.

**Procurement is waiting on Washington.** The CTO said in February 2026 that longer-dated purchases are on hold pending Treasury's FEOC guidance and that domestic batteries will not be available at scale before 2028. A buyer that will not commit to a supplier cannot be promised a delivery slot; the {{safe harbor}} and {{begin-construction deadline}} arithmetic then decides which projects keep their credits.

**The first Texas build was halved and late.** Hidden Lakes was bought as up to 450 MW / 900 MWh with operation in spring 2025, built at 220 MW / 440 MWh and operating in November 2025. No reason was published. Gunnar is the test of whether the second build holds its date.

cards.q: Lenders say GridStor 'is owned by funds managed by Goldman Sachs Asset Management'. Who are the actual owners?
cards.a: The fund's limited partners — pensions, insurers, sovereign funds. GSAM is the asset manager that runs the fund; its investment committee makes the decisions.

cards.q: What is a sponsor-created platform, and how is it different from a sponsor-backed one?
cards.a: A fund hires a team and supplies capital to build a developer from scratch (Goldman created GridStor around a project it had bought). A sponsor-backed developer existed first and sold a stake later (Blackstone into Aypa).

cards.q: Why does a fund-owned specialist buy late-stage projects rather than originate?
cards.a: A fund's clock is fixed; origination takes four to seven years and mostly produces options. Buying at ready-to-build turns the fund's money into an operating battery in about two years.

cards.q: In a tolling agreement, who decides when the battery charges and discharges?
cards.a: The toller — APS at White Tank 'may charge/discharge as needed'. The owner is paid a fixed fee for capacity and gives up the dispatch decision.

cards.q: What does a battery revenue swap do to the owner's cash flow?
cards.a: It exchanges uncertain merchant revenue on the swapped share (100 MW at Hidden Lakes) for fixed payments; the counterparty (Axpo) takes the price risk. The rest of the battery stays merchant.

cards.q: What is a development letter-of-credit facility for?
cards.a: Posting interconnection deposits and contract security across the pipeline without cash; a bank writes one for a company whose owner is a fund.

cards.q: Why does a repeat lender matter to a young developer?
cards.a: The second deal is priced on the first; NORD/LB's four GridStor transactions in three years are cheaper and faster each time — and a single point of failure if the bank's view changes.

cards.q: A pipeline of 'over 5 GW' becomes 'over 3 GW' in two months. What happened?
cards.a: Options lapsed or were dropped; a buyer's pipeline is a shopping list of acquired and optioned projects, re-scoped as they mature or fail.

cards.q: What does a tax-equity bridge loan bridge?
cards.a: The gap between construction spending and the date the credit buyer or tax-equity investor funds at commercial operation.

cards.q: Why is procurement 'un-committed' a rational choice for GridStor in 2026?
cards.a: Treasury's FEOC guidance decides which batteries keep the credit; committing to a vendor before the rule is settled risks the credit on every longer-dated project.

items.q: What kind of investor is Goldman Sachs Asset Management in relation to GridStor?
c: An asset manager running a fund whose investors own the company
items.why: GSAM manages the fund (trade press: Horizon Energy Storage); the fund's limited partners are the economic owners.

items.q: Which structure leaves the battery owner with NO dispatch decision?
items.why: Under a toll the counterparty charges and discharges as it wishes; under RA the owner still dispatches; under a swap the owner dispatches and exchanges the revenue.

items.q: How did GridStor add 250 MW of under-construction capacity in 2025?
c: Buying late-stage projects from Balanced Rock Power and Strata Clean Energy
items.why: Gunnar (Balanced Rock Power) and White Tank (Strata) were acquired near ready-to-build; every asset since 2023 was bought.

items.q: What did the Axpo agreement change about Hidden Lakes?
c: 100 MW of merchant revenue became fixed payments
items.why: The revenue swap converts part of the merchant exposure into fixed payments; Axpo takes the price risk on that share.

items.q: Which figure about the sponsor's commitment to GridStor is public?
c: A stated dollar commitment to the company
'Over $1 billion raised' for the storage strategy, per the company's media kit
items.why: No fund name, commitment or ownership split appears on any company-authored page; the media kit's fundraising line is the only figure.

items.q: Why is a 20-year toll a problem for a fund owner?
c: The fund must exit before the toll ends, so the asset will be sold on to another owner
items.why: A fund's life is ten to twelve years; the contracted asset outlives it and must be sold, at a price set by the market at that time.

items.q: What did GridStor's CTO say the company is waiting for before longer-dated procurement?
items.why: Dedrick (February 2026): 'We are now waiting for Treasury guidance before advancing pending procurement decisions on our longer-dated projects.'

items.q: Which is the only battery supplier GridStor has named?
items.why: Goleta's 44 Tesla units are the only named supply; the SolBank attribution at White Tank is an analyst's report neither party has confirmed.
